quick: Treatment 175 IU/kg SC once daily; prophylaxis 3500-4500 IU SC daily
Preferred anticoagulant; multidose vial benzyl alcohol - use preservative-free
Compatible (minimal milk transfer, not orally absorbed)
Caution; severe impairment (CrCl <30) increases accumulation - consider monitoring
Platelets (HIT), anti-Xa if needed, hemoglobin, bleeding
summary: Tinzaparin is a low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) anticoagulant given by subcutaneous injection for the treatment and prophylaxis of venous thromboembolism (deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism), including treatment in cancer-associated thrombosis and prophylaxis in surgery. It acts mainly by potentiating antithrombin-mediated inhibition of factor Xa. It carries a BOXED WARNING about spinal/epidural haematoma with neuraxial anaesthesia or spinal puncture, which can cause long-term or permanent paralysis. The multidose formulation contains benzyl alcohol, which has been associated with serious reactions ('gasping syndrome') in neonates and warrants caution in the elderly; preservative-free single-dose forms are preferred in these groups. Major risks are bleeding and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT).
indications: Treatment of acute symptomatic deep vein thrombosis with or without pulmonary embolism
Treatment of venous thromboembolism in patients with active cancer
Prophylaxis of venous thromboembolism in surgical and high-risk medical patients
Prevention of clotting in the extracorporeal circuit during haemodialysis

dosage.n: Continue at least 5-6 days and until adequately anticoagulated on a VKA (if used)

dosage.d: 3500 IU subcutaneously about 2 hours before surgery, then once daily
4500 IU once daily (or 50 IU/kg) starting peri-operatively
Use with caution; consider anti-Xa monitoring or an alternative anticoagulant
Bolus into the arterial line per protocol (e.g. ~4500 IU for a standard session)

admin: Administer by deep subcutaneous injection (e.g. anterolateral/posterolateral abdominal wall); rotate sites and do not rub
Use a preservative-free (single-dose) preparation in neonates, pregnancy and the elderly where possible (benzyl alcohol caution)
If neuraxial anaesthesia or lumbar puncture is planned, observe appropriate timing intervals before and after dosing and monitor for spinal haematoma
Do not mix with other injections; inspect the solution before use
moa: Tinzaparin is a low molecular weight heparin that binds antithrombin via a pentasaccharide sequence, accelerating antithrombin-mediated inactivation of coagulation factor Xa and, to a lesser extent, thrombin (factor IIa). Its higher anti-Xa to anti-IIa ratio gives predictable anticoagulation with less effect on the aPTT, allowing fixed weight-based dosing without routine coagulation monitoring.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to tinzaparin, heparin, pork products, or benzyl alcohol (multidose form)
History of immune-mediated heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) / positive in-vitro anti-platelet antibody test in the presence of tinzaparin
relative: Severe renal impairment (CrCl <30 mL/min) - accumulation risk
Recent neurosurgery/eye surgery, neuraxial puncture or indwelling epidural catheter
Uncontrolled severe hypertension, bleeding diathesis, peptic ulcer disease
Elderly and neonates (benzyl alcohol in multidose vial)
monitor: Platelet count (for HIT), baseline and periodically
Anti-Xa activity in renal impairment, obesity, pregnancy or where dosing is uncertain
Serum potassium with prolonged use (hyperkalaemia risk)
Neurological signs of spinal haematoma if neuraxial procedures performed

preg: LMWHs including tinzaparin are the preferred anticoagulants in pregnancy; they do not cross the placenta. Use a preservative-free (single-dose) preparation because the multidose vial contains benzyl alcohol. Dosing may need adjustment with weight changes and anti-Xa monitoring is sometimes used.
lact: Considered compatible with breastfeeding; only minimal amounts pass into milk and it is not absorbed orally by the infant.
renal: Tinzaparin is renally cleared and can accumulate in severe renal impairment (CrCl <30 mL/min), increasing bleeding risk; use with caution, consider anti-Xa monitoring or an alternative. Some data suggest less accumulation than other LMWHs, but caution still applies.
hepatic: Use with caution in hepatic impairment, which may increase bleeding risk through impaired clotting-factor synthesis; monitor for bleeding.

major: Other anticoagulants, antiplatelet agents (aspirin, clopidogrel), and thrombolytics - markedly increased bleeding risk
Neuraxial anaesthesia/spinal puncture - risk of spinal or epidural haematoma (boxed warning)
moderate: Drugs raising potassium (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, potassium-sparing diuretics) - additive hyperkalaemia risk with heparins
minor: Drugs causing thrombocytopenia may compound bleeding risk
interactions.alcohol: Avoid heavy alcohol intake, which increases bleeding risk.
interactions.diagnostics: Has little effect on aPTT; monitored by anti-factor Xa activity when needed. Can suppress aldosterone causing hyperkalaemia; may transiently raise liver transaminases.

common: Mild reversible rise in liver transaminases
serious: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT), with or without thrombosis
Spinal/epidural haematoma after neuraxial procedures (boxed warning)
Hyperkalaemia (aldosterone suppression), especially in renal impairment/diabetes
emergency: Signs of spinal haematoma (back pain, leg weakness/numbness, bladder/bowel dysfunction) - urgent imaging

monitoring: Platelet count before starting and periodically to detect HIT
Clinical signs of bleeding and haemoglobin/haematocrit
Anti-factor Xa activity in renal impairment, extremes of body weight, or pregnancy
Neurological status if neuraxial anaesthesia/puncture is used
counsel: This is a blood thinner given as an injection under the skin; you or a carer can be taught to do it
Rotate injection sites and do not rub the area; some bruising is normal
Report unusual bleeding, black stools, red/brown urine, or a lot of new bruising
Seek urgent help for back pain with leg weakness or numbness after any spinal/epidural procedure
Tell all clinicians you are on an anticoagulant before surgery, dental work or new medicines
pk: Anti-Xa activity within ~2-3 hours of subcutaneous injection
Peak anti-Xa activity about 4-6 hours after a subcutaneous dose
Anti-Xa elimination half-life approximately 3-4 hours (longer in renal impairment)
Once-daily dosing maintains anticoagulation over 24 hours
Store at room temperature; do not freeze
pearls: BOXED WARNING: spinal/epidural haematoma with neuraxial anaesthesia or spinal puncture - can cause long-term or permanent paralysis; observe timing intervals and monitor neurologically
Multidose vial contains benzyl alcohol - avoid in neonates ('gasping syndrome') and use cautiously in pregnancy and the elderly; prefer preservative-free single-dose forms
Once-daily, weight-based dosing for treatment; routine coagulation monitoring usually unnecessary - use anti-Xa (not aPTT) when monitoring is needed
Check platelets to detect HIT; never use if there is a history of HIT
Protamine only partially reverses LMWH; accumulates in severe renal impairment
missed: Inject a missed dose as soon as you remember on the same day; if it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed one and continue the schedule - do not give two doses together. Keep injections about 24 hours apart for once-daily regimens.
overdose: Overdose causes excessive anticoagulation and bleeding. Protamine sulfate partially neutralises the anti-Xa effect (it incompletely reverses LMWH); give protamine for serious bleeding and provide supportive care, transfusion and local haemostasis as needed. Monitor anti-Xa and clinical bleeding.
